# Handoff to forever-addon-dev — measured client facts, 2026-09-18

Outbound leg of the bridge described in the root README. Everything below was measured in a
live client by **this** repo and is offered to the plugin repo to record. Nothing here has
been written into `forever-addon-dev`; classification and placement belong to a session in
that repo working under its own role and authority.

**Do not edit this file to reflect what was recorded.** It is a snapshot of what was handed
over. If a finding is rejected or reworded there, that repo's copy is authoritative.

## Provenance

| | |
|---|---|
| Client | 1.60.1, build 69913, toc 16001 |
| Measured | 2026-09-18, 21:34–21:53 |
| Machine | RTX 5080, 1920x1080, D3D12, `gxMaximize=1` (maximized windowed) |
| Instrument | `AmbianceCost` addon in this repo, `addons/AmbianceCost/` |

Out of combat in all five runs. None of this was measured mid-fight.

## 1. Frame-limit checkboxes do not zero their CVar

The strongest candidate for the restriction list, because it silently produces wrong
conclusions rather than an error.

With **Max Foreground FPS** and **Target FPS** both unticked in the graphics panel and the
client running at 274 fps:

```
maxFPS = 120        useMaxFPS = 0
targetFPS = 60      useTargetFPS = 0
maxFPSBk = 30       useMaxFPSBk = 1
```

The slider value and the enable flag are **separate CVars**. `maxFPS` retains the last slider
position whether or not the limit is active. An addon reading `maxFPS` alone concludes the
client is capped at 120 when it is uncapped.

This is the same pairing already recorded for HDR in §P.22 — `HDRBrightness` /
`useHDRBrightness`, `HDRPeakBrightness` / `useHDRPeakBrightness` — which suggests a general
client convention rather than a one-off: **a `use<Name>` boolean governs whether `<Name>`
applies.** Worth stating as a convention so the next addon checks for it by default.

Also note the panel's slider minimum is 8 FPS, so there is no way to express "unlimited"
through the slider; unticking the box is the only path. `useMaxFPSBk = 1` is unrelated and
applies only when the window is unfocused.

Confidence: **high** — read directly, cross-checked against an observed 274 fps.
Not verified: whether writing `useMaxFPS` from an addon takes effect. Only reads were done.

## 2. `C_Map.GetPlayerMapPosition` returns an object and allocates 1864 bytes per call

Present and working. Returns a position **object exposing `GetXY()`**, not two numbers, and
not a plain `{x, y}` table.

| | |
|---|---|
| Cost | 4.38 – 5.71 µs per call (n=5) |
| Allocation | **1864 bytes per call**, identical in all five runs |

1864 bytes is far above a bare table and is the dominant cost of reading player position on
this client — six times the cost of a `SetCVar` write and, in garbage terms, the only figure
that constrains design. Polling every frame at 120 fps is ~218 KB/s; at 274 fps, ~500 KB/s.

Consequence for any addon that tracks position: **poll on an accumulator, not per frame.**
At 10 Hz the same work is ~18 KB/s.

Confidence: **high** — five replications, byte-identical allocation figure each time.
Not verified: behaviour inside instances (retail returns nil there); the addon guards for it
but never exercised the guard.

## 3. `C_Map.GetBestMapForUnit` is present and cheap

0.61 – 0.64 µs per call (n=5), returns a numeric uiMapID. Notably ~8x cheaper than
`GetPlayerMapPosition` and it allocates nothing measurable, but it is still a map-tree lookup
and belongs behind a zone-change event rather than in a per-frame path.

Confidence: **high**.

## 4. `SetCVar` per-call cost, extending §P.22

§P.22 records that 442 writes over 4 s produced no frame-gap spike. That is a ceiling, not a
cost. The per-call figures:

| Write | Cost |
|---|---|
| `SetCVar` with a **changed** value | 0.79 – 0.82 µs (n=5) |
| `SetCVar` with the **same** value | 0.30 – 0.32 µs (n=5) |

Both via `C_CVar.SetCVar` on `Brightness`. A changed value costs ~2.6x a no-op write, which
means the client is doing real work on change but that the work is still sub-microsecond —
comfortably affordable at any frame rate. The existing "cheap live post-process" conclusion
holds and now has a number attached.

Confidence: **high**.

## 5. `OnUpdate` elapsed is quantised to 1 ms

Every frame-gap percentile across all five runs came back a whole number of milliseconds
(`p50 = 4.000`, `p99 = 6.000`, `max = 123.000`, …). The `elapsed` argument this client passes
to an `OnUpdate` script has **1 ms resolution**.

Two consequences worth recording:

- Frame-rate-independent easing on `elapsed` still works — the quantisation is far below the
  time constants involved.
- **`OnUpdate` elapsed cannot be used to measure anything costing less than ~1 ms.** Any
  addon profiling itself this way will produce noise. `debugprofilestop` is the instrument
  with the resolution, and it is available (see 6).

Confidence: **high** — n=5, ~7000 frame samples, no fractional value observed.

## 6. Profiling and GC primitives are available

Confirmed working, which is what made everything above measurable:

- `debugprofilestart()` / `debugprofilestop()` — microsecond resolution
- `collectgarbage("count")`, `("stop")`, `("restart")`, `("collect")`

Worth an API-reference note if the plugin repo tracks tooling availability; an addon author
otherwise has no reason to assume these survived into this client.

Confidence: **high**.

---

## Do not record: the frame-gap phase data

`AmbianceCostDB.runs[*].phases` contains fps and frame-gap percentiles for three workloads
per run. **It is not evidence of anything and should not be quoted.** Two defects, both in
the instrument, not the client:

- Phases run once, in a fixed sequence, so drift across the ~30 s run loads entirely onto the
  later phases. Run 5 reported control 238.8 fps, naive 214.0, tuned 190.2 — but `tuned`
  polls 22x less often than `naive` for the same number of writes and cannot cost more. That
  ordering is drift.
- The first frames of a phase are not discarded, so the do-nothing control carries a
  72–136 ms max gap in every run, which flatters every phase measured after it.

The one thing those phases do support: **no phase in any run produced a frame gap a player
would feel.** Everything quantitative should come from the microbench.

## If the plugin repo wants this reproducible in-repo

None of the above needs the AmbianceCost addon to stay alive — but if these numbers should be
re-checkable against future builds, the natural home is a `/fprobe` subcommand alongside
`video`, built on the same `videoRamp` scaffolding (snapshot, `pcall` every setter, restore,
`C_Timer` fallback). The pieces worth lifting from `addons/AmbianceCost/AmbianceCost.lua`:

- `autoBench` — sizes iterations to a time budget so an expensive call cannot drop a 200 ms
  hitch on the frame it is measured in
- `allocPerCall` — stops the collector first, otherwise a collection inside the loop reads as
  a negative delta and the answer comes back "allocates nothing"
- `readPos` — handles all four return shapes and reports which one fired

That is a suggestion about reuse, not a request. This repo does not edit the plugin's
reference or restriction list.
